approach_variants.name: North side — Stuart Lake TH via Mountaineer Creek
approach_variants.season: Jun to mid-Jul is the sweet spot; workable through Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Park at the Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 (Eightmile Road) out of Leavenworth and walk the Stuart Lake Trail up Mountaineer Creek. At the signed split roughly two miles along, ignore the Colchuck Lake branch on the right and carry straight on. A short distance further you leave maintained tread altogether, well before Stuart Lake, ford Mountaineer Creek and follow its south fork upstream cross-country. Late in the season there is a cairned climbers' path through much of this; early in the season there is not, and the creek runs hard.

Above the streamside travel a steep, unstable talus and boulder slope lifts you into the hanging basin under Sherpa Peak and the Sherpa Glacier. This basin holds the usual bivies. From it you angle up onto the glacier bench beneath the ridge.

This is the shorter, lower-gain way in and it puts you at the toe with the most in the tank, but it commits you to a car shuttle: the standard descent is the Cascadian Couloir, which spills out on the far side of the range at Ingalls Creek. Parties report the shuttle drive between the two trailheads costing several hours round trip. In June and early July the Sherpa Glacier is a reasonable way back down to this side and removes the shuttle problem — later in the summer it is not.

There is running snowmelt near the toe of the ridge (reported around 47.48095, -120.89454); above the 8,200 ft notch there is no reliable water once the last snow patch there melts out.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are climbing the COMPLETE North Ridge, which begins at about 6,700 ft — roughly 1,500 ft of roped ground below the point where most people who say 'North Ridge' actually start. The toe is the lowest rock of the rib that separates the two glaciers: Stuart Glacier on its west side, Ice Cliff Glacier on its east. Standing at the base with the Ice Cliff Glacier and its seracs on your left and the Stuart Glacier hidden around the corner to your right, you are in the right place. If you are underneath hanging ice you have drifted too far east onto the Ice Cliff side and need to come back west to the rib's lowest rock.

The feature to NOT mistake for the start is the notch at 8,200 ft. That notch is obvious — a saddle in the crest with a scatter of bivy platforms and, usually, a small lingering snowfield for water — and it is where the Upper (original) North Ridge begins. It is reached by a rock gully climbed from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at about 7,700 ft, on the ridge's west flank. If you find yourself scrambling a gully up from snow toward a bivy saddle, you have skipped the lower 1,500 ft and are on the Upper route, not the Complete.

In cloud, use the glaciers rather than the rock: the toe is where the moraine/snow of the basin runs out against the first continuous rock, and the ice above and left of you belongs to the Ice Cliff Glacier. The 8,200 ft notch is above and right of that, reached only after the ridge has already risen well above the ice.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek and its south fork run high and fast in early-season melt
Loose talus and boulder slope below the Sherpa Glacier basin — poor footing, rockfall onto parties below
Serac and icefall exposure if you drift east under the Ice Cliff Glacier
No reliable water above the 8,200 ft notch once its snow patch is gone
Committing: standard descent exits on the opposite side of the range, so a shuttle or a very long walk-around is required

approach_variants.name: South side — Esmeralda TH over Ingalls Pass and Goat Pass
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the traverse under the Stuart Glacier has melted or consolidated
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737), take the Ingalls Way trail over Ingalls Pass, past Ingalls Lake, and continue toward the foot of Stuart's West Ridge. From there contour northwest to Goat Pass, then traverse east beneath the Stuart Glacier, staying above the large moraine mound, and aim for the toe of the ridge.

About 2,000 ft of the day is descent, so the round trip is more work than the raw gain suggests, and parties consistently report it taking longer than planned — budget eight hours and expect route-finding on the traverse rather than tread.

The reason to accept the longer, higher approach is that it removes the shuttle entirely. The Cascadian Couloir descent drops to Ingalls Creek on this side, so a party that walked in from Esmeralda walks out to its own car. Parties who came in from the north do not.

How much snow remains on the Goat Pass traverse is the recurring gear question here: sections have been reported at around 40 degrees, and whether you need an axe and traction changes week to week through the summer. Recent photos and current reports are worth more than any fixed answer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Coming from Goat Pass you arrive at the ridge from below and to the WEST, which is the opposite side from the northern approach — so the Ice Cliff Glacier is not your handrail here, the Stuart Glacier is. Keep the Stuart Glacier snow on your left as you traverse east and stay above the big moraine mound; the toe of the Complete ridge is the first continuous rock the traverse runs into, at about 6,700 ft.

The decision point is unmissable once you know to look for it: from the edge of the Stuart Glacier at roughly 7,700 ft a rock gully leads up the ridge's west side to the notch at 8,200 ft. Taking that gully puts you on the Upper North Ridge and skips the lower 1,500 ft. Continuing the traverse past and below it, down to the lowest rock, is what starts the Complete route. In poor visibility: if the snow you are standing on is still rising to your right toward a saddle, you are too high; the toe is below, where the snow ends.
hazards: Snow slopes on the Goat Pass traverse reported near 40 degrees; conditions change through the summer
~2,000 ft of descent on the way in, all of which must be regained on the way out
Long day with no bail-out once past Goat Pass
Approach consistently underestimated; parties arrive at the toe late and tired

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — summer scramble
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep, once the couloir has melted to talus
approach_variants.notes:
Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road (FR 9737) to the Esmeralda Basin road-end parking at about 4,243 ft. A quarter mile of old mining road leads to a fork; take the right branch for Longs Pass. The trail climbs an open, south-facing hillside with essentially no shade — in July and August this is a pre-dawn start, not a preference.

Longs Pass sits around 6,200-6,250 ft, roughly 2,000 ft above the car in about two miles, and it is the single most useful place on the whole approach (see baseFinding). From the pass, drop the steep loose scree on the north side, losing 1,200-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft.

Cross the creek — there is a summer log crossing, and in high melt it is worth walking to find it rather than wading — then follow the Ingalls Creek Trail upvalley (east) about a mile to the meadow and camps below the couloir's outlet. Good camps sit on the valley floor more or less straight south of where the couloir comes down, with a few more near the footlog. From camp a climbers' path threads the meadow to the toe of the couloir.

This is also the standard descent for the North Ridge, West Ridge and most of the rest of Stuart, so expect to share it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Look at the mountain from Longs Pass and settle the line there. It is the only point on the approach where the entire south face is laid out in front of you, and once you have dropped to the valley floor at 4,800 ft the couloir's mouth is one of several timbered gully mouths that all look alike from below and from inside the trees.

What you are aiming for: the couloir bottoms out in the meadow at roughly 4,800 ft, upvalley (east) of where the Longs Pass trail meets Ingalls Creek, and a beaten climbers' path leaves the meadow directly into it. It is a wide, sandy, scree-floored trough rather than a narrow cleft, and it runs unbroken for about 4,000 ft.

The confirmation that you are in the right gully comes about two thirds of the way up: a permanent snowfield around 8,800 ft, just south of the false summit. The established talus path passes it on the CLIMBER'S LEFT. Parties who take the right-hand side of that snowfield end up on much harder ground and have found old rappel-station remnants there — that is the tell that you have gone wrong, not a sign you are on route.

The couloir does not top out on the summit. It delivers you to the false summit at about 9,200 ft; the true summit at 9,415 ft is a class 2-3 scramble east along the ridge from there, and this is the second place parties in cloud go wrong — stopping at the false summit, or dropping off it in the wrong direction on the way down.
hazards: Sun-exposed hillside to Longs Pass with no water and no shade
Ingalls Creek can run high in early-season melt; find the summer log rather than fording blind
The couloir is loose top to bottom — sand, scree and unstable blocks; serious rockfall risk from parties above
Upper couloir braids into a maze of use-paths and cairns; genuinely confusing in cloud or at dawn/dusk
The 8,800 ft snowfield must be passed on the climber's left

approach_variants.name: Longs Pass from Esmeralda TH — spring snow climb
approach_variants.season: May-Jun as a snow route; road access is the limiting factor earlier
approach_variants.notes:
The same line, in a completely different medium. With the couloir snow-filled it is a straightforward steep snow climb rather than a scree grind, and many parties prefer it this way — but it demands axe and crampons, an early start, and a hard turnaround, because the whole thing faces south and softens fast.

FR 9737 is a gravel road that is not maintained through winter and is generally not clear until late June in a heavy year, so a genuinely early-season attempt means adding road miles on foot or ski. Check the road before committing.

The Longs Pass hillside carries avalanche exposure in winter and spring conditions, and the north-side drop to Ingalls Creek holds snow that can be firm and icy at dawn and slushy by mid-morning.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow cover the couloir reads far more clearly from the valley than it does in summer — it is the continuous white ribbon running the full height of the south face, and the timbered gully mouths that confuse people in August are buried. Still take the look from Longs Pass, because the valley-floor approach is in trees.

The 8,800 ft snowfield that is a landmark in summer is not a distinct feature when everything is snow, so the useful marker on the way up is the false summit at about 9,200 ft where the couloir ends. Do not treat topping out as summiting; the true summit is a scramble further east along the ridge.

On the descent in these conditions the risk inverts: the couloir is a glissade or boot-ski for most of its length and parties overrun themselves. Keep the axe in hand.
hazards: FR 9737 unmaintained in winter/spring — verify access before driving out
Avalanche exposure on the Longs Pass hillside and in the couloir itself
South-facing: wet-slide and rockfall risk build through the day, so an early turnaround is not optional
Firm/icy snow at dawn on the north side of Longs Pass
Uncontrolled glissade on descent

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass to upper Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep for dry rock; snow lingers on the Longs Pass north side into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Esmeralda trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road, take the Ingalls Way trail and, at the junction about half a mile in, stay right for Longs Pass rather than continuing to Ingalls Basin. Switchback up open slopes to the pass, which gives the first clear view of Stuart's west side.

Descend the steep dusty north side of the pass, losing close to 1,000 ft, and cross Ingalls Creek in the timber below. In normal summer flow this is a rock-hop; it is also the last reliable water before the ridge, so fill up.

Pick up the climbers' path heading east up the valley toward Stuart Pass. You leave it well SHORT of Stuart Pass, in the upper meadows at roughly 6,200-6,400 ft, and traverse climber's-left (north) across talus and heather benches to the foot of the ridge. There is no tread on this traverse and it is the part of the day people get wrong.

Some parties break the approach by camping near Ingalls Lake or in the upper Ingalls Creek basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is identified by counting gullies, not by elevation. Three roughly parallel gullies come down the lower west ridge; the route takes the MIDDLE one, and it is deeper than its neighbours. The confirming feature is at its foot: a single enormous block, described by everyone who has been there as the size of a house, sitting at the base of that gully. If there is no house-sized boulder, you are one gully over.

From the boulder you push up through scrub into the gully and climb up and rightward inside it. The gully ends at a notch — scramble through the notch and Long John Tower is directly in front of you, a distinct pinnacle on the crest. That sighting is the second confirmation that you took the right gully; if you top out of a gully and there is no tower, you are not on the West Ridge.

The climbing past Long John Tower goes up a chimney on the tower's LEFT — about three quarters of a pitch, with a chockstone near the bottom. (An alternative works a short dihedral with a fixed piton, or a layback further along the ledge, before regaining the crest.) Long John Tower and the exposed West Ridge Notch traverse beyond it are the two places parties most often stall for route-finding.
hazards: No maintained tread on the talus/heather traverse from the Stuart Pass trail to the ridge — several minor gullies look alike
Steep loose descent off the north side of Longs Pass; icy at dawn in early summer
Loose talus below the ridge with rockfall exposure from parties above
No water past the Ingalls Creek crossing
Descent is the Cascadian Couloir, and 'not staying right' near the top of it is a documented route-finding error

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep once the moat at the base has opened enough to step across; a snow patch can linger into early July
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead (FR 7601) to Colchuck Lake: about four miles and 2,280 ft, taking a fit party with a rack roughly three hours, four if loaded. Stay left at the signed junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail and grind the rocky switchbacks to the lake at 5,574 ft. There is a pit toilet near the south end of the lake and this is the last easy water.

Work around the east and south shore, then boulder-hop up onto the crest of the Colchuck Glacier's lateral moraine as early as you reasonably can — staying low costs you time in loose scree. Once on the moraine, turn slightly left and follow it south/southeast toward the northwest face of Dragontail, roughly in the direction of the Colchuck-Dragontail col, gaining about another 1,000 ft above the lake.

Allow roughly an hour from the lake to the moraine crest and another stretch of boulder-hopping beyond that. Parties report about four hours car-to-base moving well.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The whole face is one grey wall except for one thing, and that one thing is the start: a band of ORANGE rock low on the northwest face. Trip reports call it the orange wall, the orange rock band, or the coloured pile of rocks — it is visible from the moraine well before you get there and it is the only strongly coloured rock at the base. Walk the moraine until you are directly under it.

Second confirmation, for when the base is in cloud and you cannot see colour: a distinct black tower stands roughly 500 ft up the wall above the start. If you can see a black tower above you, the ground beneath it is the right ground.

At the base you will normally have to deal with a moat between the snow and the rock — the transition off the snow finger onto granite is where an axe earns its keep, and parties who left crampons behind have regretted it into July. Above the moat, 4th-class ledges lead up through the orange band; the climbing turns 5th class almost immediately off the deck, so if you are still walking after several hundred feet you have started somewhere else.

Do not confuse this with Backbone Ridge, which starts about 200 ft away and roughly 200 ft LOWER on the same face, on low-angle bushy ramps. If the ground in front of you is vegetated ramp systems trending left, that is Backbone. Serpentine's start is bare orange rock that goes up.
hazards: Moat between snow and rock at the base; axe and often crampons needed into early July
Loose scree and talus below the moraine crest
Rockfall on the lower route — a fatal-injury rockfall accident has occurred on the neighbouring Backbone Ridge, and parties above you are the main hazard
Afternoon thunderstorms are routine in summer on this face

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; light crampons and an axe are worth carrying earlier for the snow patch below the base and for the descent gully
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Serpentine approach as far as the moraine: Stuart Lake Trailhead, left at the junction onto the Colchuck Lake Trail, about four miles and 2,280 ft to Colchuck Lake — roughly an hour and a half of uphill from the trail junction. Fill water and use the toilet near the lake's south end; there is nothing above.

Past the campsites you drop out of the forest into large talus blocks and follow cairns, then pick up the climbers' path along the moraine, passing a small creek on your left, until the face opens up in front of you.

A perennial snow patch sits below the start; its size varies year to year and it is usually short enough that crampons and axe are a convenience rather than a necessity by midsummer. Above it, a loose gully and gravel ledges lead to the scrambling.

Parties report roughly four and a half to five and a half hours from car to the first roped pitch.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Backbone takes the rib immediately LEFT of Serpentine Arete as you face the northwest wall, and the two starts are close enough that people confuse them — about 200 ft apart, with Backbone's start roughly 200 ft LOWER on the face.

Tell them apart by what is under your feet. Serpentine starts on bare orange rock that is 5th class off the ground. Backbone starts on low-angle, LEFT-TRENDING RAMP SYSTEMS full of bushes. If you are pushing through vegetation on ramps, you are on Backbone; if you are pulling on clean orange rock immediately, you are on Serpentine.

The sequence from there is counter-intuitive and worth committing to memory before you are standing in cloud: scramble up and LEFT on the bushy ledges until you cliff out — being stopped is part of the route, not a mistake — then turn up and RIGHT and work back toward the ridge crest. Zigzagging left and right along ledges and ramps on 4th-class ground is normal here.

The end of the approach scrambling is marked unambiguously: a short 5.4 step finishing at a tree with slings on it, which lands you on a large flat terrace. That terrace is the belay for pitch 1 and is where the real climbing starts. If you have not reached a spacious platform with a slung tree just below it, you have not finished the approach.
hazards: Perennial snow patch below the base, size varies year to year
Loose gully and gravel ledges on the approach scramble
Serious rockfall exposure on the lower face; a rockfall accident has occurred here
Cliffing-out on the bushy ramps is normal but disorienting for a party expecting a clean line
The standard descent gully ices up late season, which changes it from a walk-off into a rappel

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, spring — lake frozen or partly frozen
approach_variants.season: Feb-Apr; the lake ice typically breaks up around mid-May
approach_variants.notes:
Icicle Creek Road is plowed only as far as Bridge Creek Campground at about 9.2 miles from Leavenworth, which leaves roughly 3.5 miles of road to walk, snowshoe or ski to the Stuart Lake / Mountaineer Creek trailhead at 3,400 ft. Plan for that; it is a substantial part of the day and it is why so many parties do this route on skis.

The trail follows the creek about two miles, crosses to the west side, and continues another mile to the fork. Take the left fork, cross back, and continue southeast — about five miles from the trailhead in total — to the north end of Colchuck Lake. Campsites are on the western banks.

When the lake is frozen, cross it directly. That is the fast option and it puts you under the north face in minutes rather than an hour of shore boulders. It is also a judgement call about ice, and it stops being available once break-up starts.

Once FR 7601 opens for the season the road walk disappears and the approach shortens dramatically — but by then the couloirs are usually past their best.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Triple Couloirs starts on the NORTH face, which is not where Serpentine and Backbone start. Do not follow the moraine southwest toward the Colchuck-Dragontail col — that is the northwest face and a different set of routes.

From the lake, go counter-clockwise to the SOUTH end, then head uphill aiming just a little EAST (climber's east) of the LOWEST POINT of Dragontail's north face. The face has a clear low point where it meets the basin; the entrance to the first couloir — the Hidden Couloir — sits slightly east of it, around 6,400 ft.

The visible marker is a prominent SNOW FINGER running down out of the face at that point. In poor visibility, work the base of the wall until the rock stops going down and starts going up — that low point is your reference — then move a short distance east and look for the snow tongue leading up into a cleft. The entrance itself is steep, exposed snow and sometimes ice; it is narrow enough that you will know when you are in it.

The couloir is called Hidden because it does not read as a continuous line from the lake. Do not expect to see the full route from below and pick it out; find the low point of the face first, then the snow finger, then commit.

Once in, you get roughly 800 vertical feet of 40-50 degree snow and ice before the route makes any decisions — if you have climbed several hundred feet of moderate snow inside a defined cleft, you are on it.
hazards: 3.5 miles of unplowed road each way in winter
Avalanche hazard on the approach and in the couloirs — this route needs a stable snowpack, not just cold
Crossing a frozen Colchuck Lake is an ice judgement, not a shortcut to take on faith
Steep, exposed snow with possible ice right at the couloir entrance, before any belay
5-9 hours one way from the lake means a benighting is a real outcome

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake and the Colchuck Glacier moraine
approach_variants.season: Mar-Jun, as soon as road access allows and while the couloir is continuously filled; by late summer it bares out
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead at the end of FR 7601 to Colchuck Lake — roughly four to four and a half miles and 2,200 ft, commonly two and a half hours. Before the road opens, add about four miles of Eightmile Road each way on foot or ski, which is the single biggest variable in the day.

When the lake is frozen (typically until around mid-May) parties ski or walk straight across it. Otherwise take the boot path around to the far, south side; the large flat boulder there is the usual gear-up and pack-stash spot.

From the south side, climb up and gain the lateral moraine. In spring there is often a boot pack this far and nothing beyond it. Follow the moraine crest RIGHT (west, toward the glacier) and then drop into the couloir. From the flat boulder to the couloir entrance is about an hour when trail-breaking is easy.

Overnight parties camp at the south end of the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The North Buttress Couloir rises directly out of the EDGE of the Colchuck Glacier's moraine — that relationship is the identification. From the far side of the lake you gain the moraine, follow it right, and the couloir is the first major gully the moraine runs you into. You do not traverse across the face looking for it; the moraine delivers you to its foot.

The route that gets confused with it is the NORTHEAST Couloir, which is the main north-side cleft and starts EAST of the summit. If you are working east along the base of the north side toward an obvious big cleft, you have walked past the NBC. The NBC is the one to the west, coming off the moraine.

The couloir runs about 2,000 ft from the base up to a notch. Once inside, you are in a defined gully with walls, not on an open snow slope — if the ground stays open and fanned out you are still on the moraine apron.

The moat at the entrance is the recurring problem and it changes the approach: when it has opened up, parties contour along the lateral moraine and traverse into the couloir higher rather than entering at its true base. If you cannot get from snow onto the couloir at the bottom, that traverse is the accepted workaround, not a sign you are in the wrong place.
hazards: Moat at the couloir entrance opens as the season progresses and can force a higher traverse in
Avalanche hazard on the moraine and in the couloir in spring
Four extra road miles each way before FR 7601 opens
Descent is over the back onto the Colchuck Glacier — soft afternoon snow there has been reported as slow and exhausting
Do not confuse with the Northeast Couloir, a separate route east of the summit

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, snow-covered glacier (early season)
approach_variants.season: Jun-early Jul, while the glacier is well filled and crevasses stay bridged
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trail #1599 from the FR 7601 road end for about 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.6 miles of steep switchbacks through boulders to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Call it four miles and 2,200 ft. This is the last reliable water.

Follow the boot path along the east shore to the inlet at the south end, then leave the trail. Gain the crest of the lateral moraine as early as you can — the alternative is a long session in genuinely loose scree and talus, and parties consistently report an hour of boulder-hopping through it when they stay low.

With good snow cover much of this basin, and later much of the glacier, can be glissaded on the way out, which is why parties favour the early window. Aim to be off the glacier before early afternoon: it softens badly and post-holing plus wet-slide potential make a late descent both slow and unpleasant.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This route's 'base' is the toe of the glacier, at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, and the way to know you are there is that the moraine crest you have been walking runs out against continuous snow that keeps rising ahead of you.

From the toe, take the LEFT (east) lobe of the glacier. That side passes directly beneath the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes — seeing that big northwest wall on your left is the confirmation you are on the correct lobe. You are climbing beside those routes, not on them.

The glacier is easy angle for most of its length and then steepens for the last stretch: about 100 ft of 40-degree snow immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col (Colchuck Col / Banshee Pass) at roughly 8,200 ft. If the angle has not kicked back, you are not at the col yet.

From the col the summit is northwest: 3rd-class sandy steps up to a summit plateau around 8,500 ft, then continue west and north over the plateau to the true summit at 8,705 ft. The plateau is the trap in cloud — it is broad and flat and the first high ground you reach on it is not the summit.
hazards: Loose scree and talus if you do not gain the moraine crest early
Rockfall off the surrounding faces onto the glacier, worst during the morning warm-up
Moats and thin bridging at the glacier margins
~100 ft of 40-degree snow below the col
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud
Glissading the descent is normal here and is also how people get hurt — axe in hand, clear runout

approach_variants.name: Colchuck Lake, bare-ice glacier (late season)
approach_variants.season: Aug-Sep, once the glacier has opened up and gone to bare, sun-cupped ice
approach_variants.notes:
The walk to Colchuck Lake and up the moraine is the same, and easier without snow. What changes is everything above the moraine.

By August the glacier typically melts out to hard, sun-cupped ice. It is not heavily crevassed, but crevasses and marginal moats that were bridged in June are open, and the surface no longer takes a boot step. Crampons and an axe stop being optional and a rope becomes a real consideration for the margins.

The scree and talus below the moraine is at its loosest now, and rockfall off the surrounding walls is more frequent with no snow holding things in place. The glissade descent is gone — plan on down-climbing everything you came up, which is the main reason the day gets longer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The same landmarks, read differently. The toe of the glacier is further up the basin than it was in June — glacial retreat and seasonal melt both push it back — so the moraine crest walk is longer before you meet ice.

Stay on the LEFT (east) lobe under the base of Dragontail's Serpentine and Backbone routes. Late in the season a thin crevasse zone has been reported opening on the descent side, and parties are advised to stay climber's left of it coming down.

The steepening to about 40 degrees immediately below the Colchuck-Dragontail col at roughly 8,200 ft is still the marker that you have arrived, and on bare ice it feels considerably more serious than the same slope in snow.
hazards: Bare sun-cupped ice: crampons and axe required, self-arrest unreliable
Open crevasses and moats at the glacier margins
Increased rockfall from the surrounding faces with no snow cover
No glissade descent — the day is longer at both ends
Broad summit plateau is disorienting in cloud

approach_variants.name: Lake outlet climbers' path into the west cirque
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep, once the gully and cirque talus are snow-free
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for about 2.25 miles with a log-bridge crossing of Mountaineer Creek near the 1.5-mile mark, then left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, a second log crossing, and steep rocky switchbacks to Colchuck Lake — about four miles and 2,280 ft, an hour and three quarters to two hours for a fit party carrying a rack.

The shorter of the two ways into the west cirque starts at the lake OUTLET, at the north end below the small dam. Cross there and follow a well-cairned climbers' path across the timbered hillside; it gains height quickly and deposits you on the talus field under the west face. Reckon about an hour from the lake, plus twenty to twenty-five minutes of boulder-hopping to reach the wall itself.

This is the way parties who have been there recommend, and it is the one to take unless the outlet crossing is unreasonable.

Colchuck Lake is the last water. The cirque and the route are dry.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
You are looking for the START OF THE WEST FACE ROUTE on a wall that carries half a dozen hard lines, so the useful information is what sits either side of it.

The West Face route's first pitch begins at a LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the base of the wall. That corner is the thing to find. From the talus you scramble up to a ledge and the first pitch goes from there.

Orient yourself with the neighbours: The Tempest starts LOWER than the West Face and lies to its RIGHT, taking a system of cracks up a black-streaked headwall — the black streaking is visible from the talus and is a good negative marker. The Scoop is further RIGHT again, right of both the West Face and the Tempest. Scarface climbs the large, obvious pale rock SCAR on the formation, several hundred feet right of the old northwest buttress line. If you are under black streaks or under a conspicuous scar, you are right of where you want to be.

Rack up on the talus rather than at the wall — the base is boulders and the flat ground is below.
hazards: Mountaineer Creek log bridges can be slick or partly submerged in high early-season flow
The outlet crossing below the dam is a real crossing, not a step-across
Cirque talus is loose and the boulder-hop to the wall is ankle-breaking ground
Snow can linger in the approach terrain into early summer
No water above Colchuck Lake

approach_variants.name: Southern line via the Aasgard-side slopes and the leftmost gully
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the gully holds snow into early summer
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative when you do not want to cross the outlet. Follow the lakeshore climbers' path counter-clockwise toward the slopes below Aasgard Pass, then cut north through a band of slide alder — look for cairns, because this is a genuine bushwhack — and climb the LEFTMOST gully about 1,000 ft to its top. From there contour east on easy ground into the cirque.

An hour and a half to two hours from the lake, more gain than the outlet line and a lot more brush, but no ford. A winter/spring variation on the same idea follows a steepening gully starting near the lake's southwest edge.

In a heavy year the gully holds snow well into early summer and an axe or light traction is worth having.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
Once you contour east into the cirque, the base identification is the same as the outlet approach: find the LEFT-FACING, LIGHTLY VEGETATED CORNER at the foot of the wall, and use the black-streaked headwall of The Tempest and the pale rock scar of Scarface, both to the RIGHT, to confirm you have not drifted along the base.

The difference this way in is that you arrive in the cirque from the south, higher up, so your first sight of the wall is from the side rather than head-on. Walk out into the talus and look at the face square-on before committing to a start; foreshortened from the flank, several corners look like the corner.
hazards: Slide alder band is a real bushwhack; cairns are the only guide
1,000 ft of loose gully
Lingering snow in the gully into early summer
More elevation gain than the outlet approach
No water above Colchuck Lake

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to the Core, dry conditions
approach_variants.season: late Jul-Sep, once Aasgard Pass is bare talus
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, right onto the Colchuck Lake Trail at the signed junction, and about four miles and 2,200 ft to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft. Filter here; there is nothing simple above until the Core.

Skirt the east and south shore to the boulder field at the lake's south end and start up Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000-2,200 ft in under a mile, on what regulars fairly describe as a jenga pile. Follow the outlet drainage and stay CLIMBER'S LEFT (east) of the first band of cliffs. Veering climber's right toward the waterfall complex on Colchuck Peak's flank is the classic and repeatedly fatal error here — people have died on that side and it cliffs out easily. Near the top the path passes in front of a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much larger one; missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Cairns are everywhere on Aasgard and they mark more than one line. Trust the worn tread over the cairn.

Top out around 7,800-7,841 ft, then lose 600-700 ft east and south through the Core's tarns and slabs to Prusik Pass. In the Core there are a couple of places where it is easy to add distance without adding progress, but the navigation is not hard in clear weather.

Most parties do this car-to-car, and a fit team should expect a 20-21 hour day; the Enchantments overnight permit lottery is competitive enough that camping is not a plan you can rely on.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the highest point of Prusik Pass, do NOT go over the first bump in front of you — go AROUND it. Parties who climb straight over it lose time and, more importantly, lose the path.

Past the bump the climbing line drops out of sight. Keep scrambling easy blocky class 2 ground and it reappears. The landmark you are heading for first is a huge BALANCED, DISH-SHAPED ROCK — that is the right place to stash packs and put on shoes, and it is not yet the start of the climbing.

One more knob of scrambling past that brings you to the actual base: an OVERHANGING ROCK at the foot of the route, which is the natural sheltered spot to leave big bags.

The first pitch is the final confirmation and it is unmistakable even in cloud: a long pitch up a WIDE CRACK, about 5.6, in a conspicuously WHITE section of rock. The white band is the marker — the surrounding stone is not that colour. A distinct crack of roughly 5.6 leading up through blocky ground to the ridge is what you want; if you are staring at clean, hard, featureless granite you are on one of the south-face routes instead.

Belay at a slingable block; the 5.7 slab crux with an old piton comes above that.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: veering climber's right into the cliffed waterfall terrain has killed people
Loose talus and rockfall the full length of Aasgard, worse in the afternoon heat
Misleading and multiplying cairns on the pass and in the Core
No water between Colchuck Lake and the Core tarns
Very long day; parties routinely finish the descent of Aasgard in the dark
Descent from Prusik is rappels, not a walk-off — do not arrive without the gear

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass with snow, early season
approach_variants.season: May-early Jul, while the pass holds continuous snow
approach_variants.notes:
Same line, different problem. With snow on it, Aasgard is an axe-and-sometimes-crampons proposition rather than a talus grind, and it is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Early-season snow softens through the day into deep, punchy stuff that hides ice underneath, and the hidden creek running beneath the talus is a real hazard where snow bridges it. The consolidated dawn snow that makes the ascent quick is also the surface that makes an uncontrolled slide easy.

On the plus side the route-finding is simpler with the talus buried, and the Core beyond the pass travels fast on snow.

On the north side of Prusik itself, snow adds both hazard and time to the rappel descent — budget for it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The Prusik Pass landmarks survive the snow, because they are large rock features: go AROUND the first bump rather than over it, find the huge balanced dish-shaped rock to gear up at, then one more knob to the overhanging rock at the base.

The first pitch's white rock band and wide 5.6 crack still identify the start. What changes early season is the ground below the base — snow can cover the scrambling approach entirely, so the sequence of bump, dish rock, knob, overhang is what you navigate by rather than any boot path.
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Hidden creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges
Punchy afternoon snow concealing ice
Uncontrolled slide on the pass, ascending or descending
Snow on Prusik's north side lengthens and complicates the rappel descent

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass to Gnome Tarn
approach_variants.season: Jul-Sep; earlier the pass is a snow climb and the Core travel is on snow
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake Trailhead, Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek and up the switchbacks to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft — about four miles and 2,000-2,200 ft.

From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass: roughly 2,000 ft in a little over a mile of loose scree and dirt, and the crux of the day. Stay climber's LEFT of the cliff bands; the terrain to climber's right, toward the waterfalls on Colchuck Peak's flank, cliffs out and has killed people. Snow lingering into early July hides a creek running beneath the talus.

From the pass at 7,841 ft travel cross-country through the Core, dropping from Talisman Lake toward Rune Lake, then ascending to the gentle ridge east of Rune's upper basin to reach Gnome Tarn. Gnome Tarn is the standard camp for this face and sits close under it.

A longer approach on the Snow Lakes Trail exists and is the fallback when Aasgard or the Stuart Lake trailhead is closed; some parties deliberately go in over Aasgard and out via Snow Lakes, about 21 miles, to spare their knees a second descent of the pass.

The last stretch to the wall is unmarked cross-country over slabs and talus.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From Gnome Tarn, traverse NORTHEAST to the south face. The base of the Stanley-Burgner sits at about 7,350 ft.

The defining feature is a pair of DEEP CHIMNEYS on the face. The route starts to the LEFT of those two chimneys, in a crack system on steep WHITE granite — the base is immediately beside a left-slanting chimney. Two deep chimneys with the route just left of them is the pattern to hold in your head; if you have walked past the chimneys and are still looking, you are right of the start.

The second confirmation is vegetation. The first pitch is 5.8 up the crack system and finishes at a belay just BELOW SOME SHRUBBY PINES. From the talus, a photograph-worthy way to say it is that the route starts at the trees on the left and goes up. Pitch 2 then works up through those pines at 5.7. So: white granite, left of the two deep chimneys, aiming for a small stand of scrubby pines about a pitch up.

This face carries several routes that share the same base area and the same north-side rappel descent, so being one crack system over is easy and consequential. If your first pitch is harder than 5.8 or has no pines above it, you are on a neighbour.

Note that the West Ridge starts somewhere else entirely — around at Prusik Pass on the far side of the peak — so the two are not confusable at the base, only on the map.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain to climber's right, loose rock, fatalities on record
Hidden creek beneath the talus on the pass under early-season snow
Avalanche exposure on the pass in shoulder season
Unmarked cross-country slab and talus travel from Gnome Tarn to the base
Rappel descent on the north side is shared by several south-face routes and backs up when busy

approach_variants.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear LEFT onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up toward the broad saddle between Argonaut and Colchuck at about 7,700 ft. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is OUTSIDE the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base of the roped climbing is a NOTCH on the ridge crest, and the feature that identifies it is a single conspicuous GENDARME standing alone on the ridge. The notch you want is immediately WEST of that lone gendarme. Not east of it, not the next notch along — west, with the gendarme on your east side as you stand in it.

Getting there: from the Porcupine Creek basin or the Argonaut-Colchuck col area at about 7,700 ft, angle up snow or blocky rock to gain the crest. The southeast ridge can be crossed lower at a notch around 6,750 ft, so a notch on its own does not tell you much — the gendarme does.

In cloud, work the crest until you meet a free-standing tower, then take the gap on its west side. If you are already on knife-edge ground with exposure, you have gone past the start and are on the route.
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto Bean Creek Trail near the start
Ingalls Creek ford is a genuine obstacle in early season or after rain
Loose talus in the basin; hard snow in shoulder season warranting axe and crampons
Long, remote approach — a partial day just to reach the base, so plan a car-camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trail closures following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — verify before committing

approach_variants.name: Stuart Lake TH cross-country up Mountaineer Creek to the north basin
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; parties report significant snow and slush still hampering things into late June
approach_variants.notes:
From the Stuart Lake Trailhead, hike the Stuart Lake Trail and go STRAIGHT PAST the Colchuck Lake turnoff. Continue to about 4,700 ft, where a faint path leaves the trail for Mountaineer Creek. Follow it over and down to the creek, then up the creek to roughly 4,780 ft, and bushwhack up to a boulder field below Argonaut at about 4,925 ft.

Traverse the boulders following cairns south-southwest and cut through slide alder — this brush is the notorious part of the day, and staying on talus to climber's right where you can avoids the worst of it. Then head up in or beside the trees, through boulders, talus, scree and dry creek beds, past waterfall slabs, into the north basin below Argonaut at about 6,700 ft. Roughly four hours car-to-basin for an efficient party.

Expect to lose the boot path in the boulder field. Most of this approach is navigated by feel; there is no marked trail. Wet, mossy logs over Mountaineer Creek are a nuisance in both directions.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
From the north basin at about 6,700 ft, a SNOW FINGER runs up to the southwest. Climbing it — late in the season with some loose, dirty rock where the snow has pulled back — brings you to a small COL / NOTCH at the very foot of the Northwest Arete. That col is the start of the roped climbing.

So the sequence in poor visibility is: basin floor, single obvious snow tongue heading southwest, top of the tongue, notch. The snow finger can be firm or icy late in the season and looks more intimidating than the grade suggests — carry an axe and consider crampons even though this is a rock route.

Above the col the arete gives six to eight pitches of blocky, generally solid Class 4 to 5.6 with route-finding that is described as straightforward. If the climbing above your notch is immediately hard or featureless, you are not on the arete.

Do not plan to reverse the arete: the descent traverses off east to the Argonaut-Colchuck col with roughly four rappels, so you finish on the other side of the mountain from your packs and your approach.
hazards: Dense slide alder in the Mountaineer Creek drainage
Wet, mossy log crossings of Mountaineer Creek
Boot path disappears in the boulder field — sustained off-trail navigation
Firm or icy snow finger to the col late season
Waterfall slabs on the approach
Descent route-finding is genuinely tricky and is not a place to be in poor visibility

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass and up from Ingalls Creek
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; snow lingers on the approach benches and north-facing ground into early July
approach_variants.notes:
Esmeralda Basin / Longs Pass Trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway Road (FS-9737), about 4,300 ft. Longs Pass Trail (FST 1391) for roughly 2.3 miles and 2,300 ft to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft.

Drop the north side, losing 1,300-1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft — early season there are snow fingers here that glissade well. Ford or rock-hop the creek, join the Ingalls Creek Trail and follow it RIGHT (east) about a mile to the Beverly-Turnpike Trail junction at about 4,700 ft.

Leave the maintained trail there. Ascend rightward across the meadow to where the slope steepens at about 5,000 ft, cross the stream, and climb the rib staying LEFT of its crest. At around 5,800 ft traverse right, cross over the rib, and contour into the basin below Sherpa.

There is a flat table-rock shelf at about 7,400 ft that parties use as a bivy or gear-up spot. Around 6,000 ft the climbers' path enters a spot where the gully narrows; from there some parties gain a few hundred feet east to the divide separating that gully from the one leading more directly toward Sherpa, then drop grudgingly into the correct gully and take class 2 slopes up to the table rock.

Six to seven hours one way is typical. Water at Ingalls Creek and from snowmelt in the upper basin in season.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The landmark that settles this route is Sherpa's BALANCED ROCK — a distinctive perched block on the summit ridge, and it is visible from the basin below. Use it.

From the basin at about 7,000 ft, climb a broad gully trending NORTH-NORTHEAST to gain the ridge crest just EAST of the balanced rock. That is the correct point on the crest. From there the line runs WESTWARD over blocks and sandy benches, passing the balanced rock, to the summit — class 3-4.

So the check in cloud is: pick the crest, find the balanced block, and make sure it is to your WEST when you arrive. If the block is behind you to the east, you gained the crest too far along and are between the balanced rock and the summit rather than below it.

The flat table-rock at about 7,400 ft is the intermediate confirmation on the way up — it is a distinct flat platform in otherwise broken ground and it sits on the correct line. Do not confuse the table rock (7,400 ft, a bivy shelf) with the balanced rock (on the summit ridge, a perched block); they are different features doing different jobs.

The descent uses a rappel line back to a notch west of the technical climbing, so know where the notch is before you go up.
hazards: Steep loose drop off the north side of Longs Pass
Ingalls Creek ford runs high in early-season melt
Brushy bushwhack between the Ingalls Creek Trail and the open basin
Long boulder and talus field beneath Sherpa — a stamina and route-finding crux both
Picking the correct gully out of the basin: the obvious narrowing at ~6,000 ft is a decision point, not the line
Descent is rappels off mixed fixed slings, some reported as poor — carry cord

approach_variants.name: Esmeralda TH over Longs Pass, then east to the 8,000 ft notch
approach_variants.season: mid-Jul-Sep; the north-facing approach gully holds snow into early July
approach_variants.notes:
The approach shares everything with the West Ridge as far as the basin: Longs Pass Trail from the Esmeralda trailhead over Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft, down to Ingalls Creek at about 4,800 ft, ford, east on the Ingalls Creek Trail to the Beverly-Turnpike junction, then off-trail up the rib and into the basin beneath Sherpa.

From the basin the two routes diverge. Instead of heading for the West Ridge notch, angle climber's LEFT — east — traversing a grassy slope and then climbing a talus and scree gully toward the notch east of the summit.

This is longer and more circuitous through loose talus than the direct West Ridge line, and picking the right gully is the main problem. There is another level of basin higher and southwest of the summit; ending up in it means you have gone the wrong way. Carry a 50m rope from the notch, since the route above uses fixed slings at several obstacles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The target is a notch at roughly 8,000 ft, EAST of the true summit and about 600 vertical feet below it. Gaining the ridge crest itself happens about 100 ft ABOVE (east of) that notch, on class 2 ground — so the notch is a waypoint, and the crest is gained just past it, not in it.

From the basin the gully leading to it is the obvious one heading up toward that saddle east of the summit, and trip reports confirm that the gully that looks right from below IS the right one. The failure mode is overshooting rather than picking the wrong-looking line: parties climb too far and end up in the higher basin to the southwest of the summit.

The orientation check: at the notch the summit should be UP and to your WEST, roughly 600 ft above you. If the summit is above and east, or if you are level with the summit, you are in the wrong saddle.

Sherpa's Balanced Rock sits on the summit ridge and is visible from below — it is the West Ridge's landmark, not this route's start, but it tells you where the summit ridge runs and therefore which way to count from.

Most parties do not reverse this ridge. The accepted descent finishes near the summit, traverses to the top of the West Ridge, and uses that route's rappel line — so plan to end the day on the other side of the peak from where you started climbing.
hazards: Loose talus and scree in the approach gully
Route-finding: the higher basin southwest of the summit is the overshoot trap
Snow lingering in the north-facing gully into early July
Ingalls Creek ford and the long brushy off-trail section, same as the West Ridge
Fixed slings on the route and on the descent are weathered — carry replacement cord

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core, snow-free
approach_variants.season: late Jul-early Oct
approach_variants.notes:
Stuart Lake / Colchuck Lake Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, Stuart Lake Trail #1599 for roughly 2.5 miles to the signed fork, then left/south on the Colchuck Lake Trail for another 1.8 miles to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft, around 4.3 miles in. That is the last easy, reliable water.

Skirt the lake's south and east shore on a braided cairned path over talus and slab to the foot of Aasgard Pass, the obvious steep headwall at the lake's south end. The pass gains roughly 2,000 ft in under a mile on dirt switchbacks, loose scree and boulder-hopping. Cairns get knocked over and the path braids; there are cairns marking more than one line, so follow the most worn tread and keep climber's LEFT of the cliff bands. Drifting climber's right toward the waterfall terrain on Colchuck Peak's flank is how people get cliffed out and killed here. Near the top the path passes a small waterfall and climbs steeply beside a much bigger one — missing the turn there puts you on vertical rock.

Top out at about 7,800-7,841 ft, roughly 5.3 miles from the car. Cross the grey talus and glacial till of the upper Core past Tranquil Lake and Isolation Lake, then drop slightly into the meadow-and-tarn complex sometimes called the Brisingamen Lakelets.

Late September brings the larches, and with them the year's heaviest crowds and permit competition. A day scramble needs no lottery permit; camping in the Core does.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
There are two separate 'find it' problems on this route and the first one is the trail junction, not the mountain.

Near the FAR END of the meadows, watch for an UNSIGNED path forking RIGHT (west) toward Little Annapurna. It is a use-path, not tread. The unambiguous overshoot marker is downstream of it: if you cross a small stream AND pass a sign for the toilet, you have gone too far and need to come back. That pair — stream then toilet sign — is the single most useful navigational fact on this route, because the junction itself has nothing to see.

From the pass at Aasgard, Little Annapurna lies to the SOUTHEAST and reads as a gently rolling hill rather than a peak, which is part of why people walk past the turn.

The second problem is the mountain itself, and the honest answer is that there is no single line. The 'route' is a scatter of well-worn boot paths over broad south-facing slabs and talus. Cairns are present, easy to lose, and mark more than one option. The working rule reported by everyone: take the path of least resistance up the peak's LEFT (east) side, switchbacking and scrambling, nothing harder than low 3rd class, to the summit at 8,485 ft.

If you find yourself on anything that feels like real climbing, you have drifted off the line — this is a walk-up with hands occasionally on rock, and any steepening means come back left and lower.
hazards: Aasgard Pass: cliffed-out terrain climber's right near the waterfalls, with fatalities on record
Misleading and duplicated cairns on the pass and on the peak itself
Loose rock and rockfall from parties above, on the pass and on the final slopes
No water past the Colchuck Lake outlet
Full sun and thunderstorm exposure on open talus above the pass — no shelter anywhere in the Core

approach_variants.name: Aasgard Pass and the Core with snow
approach_variants.season: late Jun-mid Jul, and shoulder season either side
approach_variants.notes:
The same line with snow on the pass and on the upper slopes. An ice axe is worth carrying, and sometimes crampons, even though the peak itself is a scramble — the exposure is on Aasgard, not on Little Annapurna.

Early-season snow on the pass firms overnight and turns punchy through the day, hiding ice underneath; there is also a creek running beneath the talus that snow bridges. The pass is avalanche terrain in shoulder season.

Descending the pass in the afternoon on softened snow, with tired legs and other parties below, is the well-documented incident scenario here. Glissade only where there is a genuine clean chute with a safe runout — by mid to late summer the pass is bare talus and there is nothing to glissade.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
With snow covering the Core, the unsigned right-hand fork toward Little Annapurna and the stream-then-toilet-sign overshoot marker are all buried or unreliable, so navigate by the lakes instead: from the top of Aasgard, travel between Isolation Lake and Tranquil Lake and then head SOUTH toward the broad rolling summit mass that sits southeast of the pass.

On the peak, snow simplifies the problem — the braided boot paths and contradictory cairns that make the summer scramble confusing are gone, and the broad south-facing slopes go directly. Keep to the LEFT (east) side of the mountain and take the easiest angle available.

What to watch for instead: the transition from snow to bare slab, which happens patchily on a south-facing slope in early summer and is where an unroped slip becomes a slide.
hazards: Avalanche terrain on Aasgard Pass in shoulder season
Creek running beneath the talus under snow bridges on the pass
Punchy afternoon snow over hidden ice
Patchy snow-to-slab transitions on the summit slopes
Uncontrolled glissade descending the pass — the classic afternoon incident here
